claims.text: The multicomponent nature of high-entropy alloys creates severe atomic-scale disorder.
Atomic-scale disorder in HEAs causes sluggish diffusion of metal cations and oxygen anions.
Reduced ionic diffusion promotes selective oxidation of Cr or Al.
Selective oxidation of Cr or Al forms Cr2O3 or Al2O3 scales.
The resulting oxide scale is dense, adherent, and self-healing.
A dense, adherent oxide scale protects the underlying alloy from further oxidation.
A suitable high-temperature HEA contains oxide-forming elements such as Cr, Al, or Si together with refractory metals.
The proposed initial HEA has a stable phase structure in the as-cast or homogenized condition.
High-temperature oxidation produces a continuous, thin, and adherent scale dominated by Cr2O3 or Al2O3.
The scale's grain size, porosity, and interfacial integrity are governed by diffusion inhibition arising from high configurational entropy.
High atomic disorder increases the kinetic barriers to outward metal-cation migration and inward oxygen-anion migration.
Sluggish ionic diffusion limits oxide-scale growth.
Limiting rapid scale thickening reduces spallation and enhances oxide adhesion.
Selective oxidation of high-oxygen-affinity elements continuously renews the protective barrier.
The HEA will have a lower oxidation rate and lower weight gain than a lower-entropy baseline under identical oxidation conditions.
The HEA will form a thinner, more continuous, and more adherent scale than the lower-entropy baseline.
The HEA will retain its underlying alloy microstructure better than the lower-entropy baseline after high-temperature exposure.
The lower configurational entropy of the baseline alloy causes faster diffusion.
Faster diffusion in the baseline produces a thicker, more porous, and less adherent oxide scale.

The proposed mechanism applies up to about 1200 °C at moderate oxygen partial pressure, while more extreme atmospheres or substantially higher temperatures may introduce different oxidation kinetics or phase changes.
